title: Service-level graceful degradation and orchestrated fallback playbook
author: Priya Nair
summary: Playbook describing service-level graceful degradation modes and automated orchestrated fallback strategies for Private deployments. Targets production SLOs, operator run steps, automation rules, and rollback/rehydration guidance for VPC and on-prem installations.
overview:
Purpose:
This document defines a canonical operational playbook for gracefully degrading inference services and orchestrating fallbacks in Private (VPC and on-prem) deployments. It addresses both automated and operator-driven responses when a service, model instance, or infrastructure tier breaches latency, error, or capacity thresholds. The goal is to preserve availability and cost predictability while minimizing user-visible regressions.

Scope:
- Applies to Redwood Private control plane + runtime bundles (node-agent, model-router, model-worker, kv-cache, tracing-collector)
- Covers both host-level and model-serving degradations
- Assumes standard telemetry and tracing integrations (Prometheus metrics, Grafana, Tempo traces, centralized logs)

Audience:
- SREs and Platform Engineers supporting Private installs
- Field engineering teams doing onboarding or handoff

Key principles:
- Fail closed on data safety, fail open on availability when configured by the customer
- Prefer deterministic, reversible steps with automated guardrails
- Use progressively impactful remediation: soft-degrade -> model-variant fallback -> routing offload -> capacity eviction -> operator rollback
triggers:
Primary automated triggers (examples):
- High-latency spike: model-router.p95_latency > 1200ms for 1 minute AND model-worker.err_rate > 1%
- Throughput saturation: node-agent.request_queue_depth > 500 for > 2m OR node_cpu_utilization > 92% for 3m
- Cache thrash: kv-cache.miss_rate > 40% AND kv-cache.latency_p95 > 50ms
- Elevated downstream errors: external-store.errors_total incrementing AND model-worker.timeouts > 5%

Secondary operator triggers: ongoing customer complaints, QBR-discovered regressions, or core dump events on model-worker.
degradation_modes:
Defined degradation modes (ordered by impact):
1) Soft response shaping (least impact)
- Purpose: reduce per-request token work and tail latency without changing model variant.
- Actions: enforce per-request max_tokens=128, enable response-truncation plugin, set sampling temperature to 0.6 for non-core routes.
- When to use: brief latency spikes under 10m.

2) Prefix/KV cache priming and aggressive reuse
- Purpose: increase cache hit ratio to lower token compute.
- Actions: enable block-level prefix caching, increase kv-cache.eviction_threshold to 80%, extend KV TTL from 30s -> 180s for stable routes.
- Risk: stale conditional outputs for stateful sessions; only enabled for idempotent routes.

3) Model-variant fallback (preferred automated fallback)
- Purpose: route requests to a compatible, lower-cost/latency model variant (quantized or smaller topology).
- Actions: model-router updates routing table to prefer model-v1-lite then model-v1-quant if v1-full cross-SLO. Update request headers: x-rw-fallback-reason.
- Validation: check syntactic compatibility with function-calling and tool contracts.

4) Route-level shedding / throttling
- Purpose: protect core business traffic by throttling best-effort routes.
- Actions: apply per-route rate-limits, enable token-bucket fairness for tenant classes, downgrade free-tier keys to background queue.

5) Capacity eviction and autoscale failover (most disruptive)
- Purpose: reclaim GPU/CPU for critical services and activate reserved capacity.
- Actions: cordon non-critical nodes, trigger reserved GPU pool warmup, preempt batch workloads, migrate stateful model shards to hot nodes.
orchestration_playbook:
Automated orchestration example (high-level):
1) Detection -> escalate to orchestration controller (sentinel) when trigger fires
2) Controller evaluates remediation candidates (soft-shape -> cache -> model-variant -> shedding) and scores by risk + expected latency reduction
3) Controller applies lowest-risk action with canary fraction 10% for 2 minutes; monitor for regressions
4) If canary improves SLOs, increment to 50% for 5 minutes, then 100% and close incident.
5) If regression observed, rollback to previous state and evaluate next candidate.

Operator runbook (manual escalation):
1) Confirm alert and gather metrics: run diagnostics (CLI):
- rwctl metrics query --service model-router --range 5m --metrics p95,err_rate,queue_depth
- rwctl node list --status NotReady

2) Enter incident channel and assign roles: incident_commander, fallback_owner, customer_liaison.

3) Apply soft-shape:
- rwctl route update --route /chat --max_tokens 128 --priority high

4) Prime KV cache for heavy routes:
- rwctl kv cache-prime --route /search --sample 1000 --ttl 180s

5) Promote model-variant fallback (if canary allowed):
- rwctl routing promote --route /chat --from model-v1-full --to model-v1-lite --weight 10
- Monitor: 
  - grafana dashboard: Private->Model Routing->Latency by variant
  - tracing: look for function_call errors or serialized mismatch

6) If fallback successful, document customer-facing changelog and update rollout policy record.

CLI and YAML example (routing promotion):
```yaml
apiVersion: redwood/v1
kind: FallbackPolicy
metadata:
  name: chat-latency-fallback
spec:
  route: /chat
  triggers:
    - metric: model-router.p95_latency
      operator: ">"
      value: 1200
      window: 60s
  actions:
    - type: model_variant_promote
      target: model-v1-lite
      canary_percent: 10
      rollback_on: err_rate>0.5%
```
rollback_procedure:
Principles:
- Rollbacks must be fast and state-safe. Prioritize in-place config rollbacks before model re-deploys.
- Always record the exact routing table and node assignments before change.

Rollback steps (common scenarios):
A) Rolling back a routing promotion:
1) rwctl routing set-weight --route /chat --variant model-v1-full --weight 100
2) rwctl routing set-weight --route /chat --variant model-v1-lite --weight 0
3) Verify p50/p95 and error rates for 10m.

B) Rolling back a KV cache TTL increase (stale data risk):
1) rwctl kv set-config --route /search --ttl 30s --eviction_threshold 70%
2) Force key invalidation for impacted session IDs: rwctl kv invalidate --route /search --selector session:stale

C) Eviction rollback (when preemption caused regressions):
1) Uncordon nodes: rwctl node uncordon <node-id>
2) Rebalance model-shards: rwctl model rebalance --policy conservative
3) Re-enable batch jobs with controlled ramp-up: rwctl batch enable --jobs <id> --rate 20%/m

Post-rollback tasks:
- Create incident postmortem with timeline and metrics
- Add regression tests to eval harness for the trigger case
verification_and_smoke_tests:
Smoke checklist after each change (operator or automation):
- SLOs: model-router.p95_latency < 800ms for core routes; error_rate < 0.5%
- Functional correctness: run 100 synthetic queries from private-telemetry runner and validate schema + function-call success
- End-to-end: run sample customer prompt set for 5 tenants and validate token-cost delta < +15%

Automated test examples:
- rwctl test run --suite fallback-sanity --tenants 5 --duration 10m
- CI hook: change to FallbackPolicy definition must pass "fallback-sim" regression tests (locally simulated 10k req/min)
ownership_and_escalation:
Roles and responsibilities:
- Incident Commander: oncall SRE (primary) — coordinates communication and approves high-impact actions
- Fallback Owner: platform engineer (secondary) — executes routing, model promotions, and cache changes
- Customer Liaison: Solutions Engineer — communicates status and temporary mitigations to the customer
- Control Plane Owner: infra-platform lead — approves capacity eviction and reserved-pool usage

Escalation matrix:
- 0-10m: oncall SRE handles.
- 10-30m: notify platform lead and solutions engineering.
- >30m or SLA breach: engage engineering manager and customer success; prepare formal incident report.
telemetry_and_alerting:
Essential SLIs and alert thresholds:
- model-router.p95_latency (SLO target: 500ms, alert: >1200ms for 1m)
- model-worker.error_rate (SLO target: <0.2%, alert: >1% for 2m)
- kv-cache.miss_rate (baseline <20%, alert: >40% for 3m)
- node_cpu_utilization (alert: >92% for 5m)

Example Prometheus rule (text):
- alert: ModelRouterHighP95
  expr: increase(model_router_p95_ms[1m]) > 1200
  for: 1m
  labels:
    severity: page
  annotations:
    summary: "Model router p95 high (>1200ms)"

Dashboards to monitor:
- Private -> Per-tenant SLO overview
- Model routing: variant comparison by latency, cost, and error rate
- KV cache health: hit/miss, TTL histogram, eviction churn
config_table:
| Component | Default setting | Degradation override | Notes |
|-----------|-----------------|----------------------|-------|
| model-router | p95_target=500ms | p95_target=800ms during soft-shape | Use for short spikes |
| kv-cache | ttl=30s, eviction=65% | ttl=180s, eviction=80% for idempotent routes | Only for read-heavy routes |
| node-agent | request_queue=200 | queue=100 (throttle) | Protect CPU-bound nodes |
| autoscaler | scale_down_delay=10m | fast-scale-down disabled during incident | Prevent flapping |

notes:
History and rationale:
- Created after two field incidents where quantized fallbacks were applied with no canary and customer workloads experienced silent semantic regressions.
- This playbook enshrines a canary-first promotion pattern and explicit KV-cache safety checks.

Change log:
- 2027-02-02: Added automated scoring criteria for remediation candidates and new CLI commands for cache priming.
- 2026-11-10: Initial draft and internal review.
